textBlocks: At Cloudworx Studio, I worked on a live cricket ball trajectory visualizer for StanceBeam, built for match analysis and broadcast.

sections.content: At Cloudworx Studio, I worked on a live cricket ball trajectory visualizer for StanceBeam, built for match analysis and broadcast.

sections.caption: Ball trajectory and broadcast overlay in the cricket visualizer.
sections.alt: Ball trajectory and broadcast overlay in the cricket visualizer.

sections.content: StanceBeam developed an ML-based system to track a cricket ball during live matches. Our application received trajectory data through an API and turned it into animations. The visualization needed to be compelling for live telecasts and accurate enough to support analysis of Leg-Before-Wicket (LBW) decisions.
Interface and animation controls

We built the application with React and React Three Fiber. My primary role was developing the 2D interface with Tailwind CSS. Operators could choose the animation type, select an over and ball, and configure camera transitions and displayed data. I also designed and animated the ticker overlay. Once the scene was set up, pressing the spacebar started the animation.

projectDetails.title: Training Simulation Application for the Logistics Industry
projectDetails.imageAlt: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.
textBlocks: During my sixth-semester internship at Hoansi Studios, I developed a browser-based warehouse training prototype for the logistics industry.
The simulation combines 3D navigation, box handling, scanner input, and real-time instructions with an editor for configuring training exercises.

modal.title: Training Simulation Application for the Logistics Industry

sections.content: During my sixth-semester internship at Hoansi Studios, I developed a browser-based warehouse training prototype for the logistics industry.

sections.caption: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.
sections.alt: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.

sections.content: The training problem

COVID-19 restrictions limited the number of workers who could be on a warehouse floor. Training new workers on-site could therefore reduce warehouse productivity. The client proposed a virtual training module to reduce the time needed for on-site training. This was the goal of the prototype, rather than a measured outcome.

The requirements were an immersive 3D environment, interaction with warehouse equipment, real-time instructions and feedback, customizable task sequences, and access through a browser without local installation.
From A-Frame to Three.js

I first built the receiving workflow in A-Frame to test movement and scanning interactions. That version distinguished between pallets and individual boxes. I then modeled a warehouse in Autodesk Fusion 360 and made its textures and floor markings in Photoshop and Illustrator.

images.caption: The early A-Frame proof of concept.
images.alt: The early A-Frame proof of concept.

images.caption: Warehouse modeling and layout.
images.alt: Warehouse modeling and layout.

sections.content: With the model ready, I moved development to Three.js. I added gaze-based box dragging and dropping, text input for the scanner, and interactions that simulated the receiving workflow.
Configuring an exercise

The setup editor lets an instructor add or remove the printer step, set the number of boxes and their drop-off points, and choose which boxes produce a scan error. A scan error prompts the trainee to enter the information manually.

sections.caption: The setup editor for configuring a training exercise.
sections.alt: The setup editor for configuring a training exercise.

projectDetails.title: Fare Calculation Algorithm Simulator
projectDetails.imageAlt: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.
textBlocks: For my 2021 pre-thesis project, I researched auto-rickshaw drivers in Bangalore and prototyped a simulator for exploring fare calculation models.
Users configure fuel cost, per-kilometer rate, base fare, and minimum distance, then follow average fares, take-home earnings, and fuel expenses.

sections.content: For my 2021 pre-thesis project, I researched auto-rickshaw drivers in Bangalore and prototyped a simulator for exploring fare calculation models.

sections.caption: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.
sections.alt: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.

sections.content: Algorithms and everyday work

Service aggregation apps use algorithms to assign work and calculate pay. Small changes to these systems can have significant effects on the daily lives of gig workers. I wanted to understand those effects in the context of auto-rickshaw drivers.

Coming from Mumbai, where meter regulations were strictly enforced, I found the situation in Bangalore very different. I interviewed 20 drivers from different parts of Bangalore, often with a translator, to understand their perspectives on fares and ride-sharing platforms.
The prototype

The simulator models auto-rickshaws picking up and dropping off passengers within a fixed area. I integrated the Google Maps API and made fare variables configurable, allowing users to observe how different settings affect earnings and expenses over time.
What the research revealed

Mathematical optimization can suggest an ideal fare model, but interviews showed that social and political factors often diverge from purely numerical solutions. The project helped me examine where a simulation can be useful and where lived experience complicates its assumptions.

projectDetails.title: Plastic Sweeper — Live Interactive Data Visualization
projectDetails.imageAlt: Plastic Sweeper: an ocean pollution visualization inspired by Minesweeper.
textBlocks: Plastic Sweeper is a Minesweeper-inspired game I made in a 2019 studio led by Garret Lynch to communicate the scale of plastic pollution in the oceans.

modal.title: Plastic Sweeper — Live Interactive Data Visualization
modal.context: Third-semester studio · 2019 · Featured in the p5.js 2020 showcase

sections.content: Plastic Sweeper is a Minesweeper-inspired game I made in a 2019 studio led by Garret Lynch to communicate the scale of plastic pollution in the oceans.

sections.caption: Plastic Sweeper: an ocean pollution visualization inspired by Minesweeper.
sections.alt: Plastic Sweeper: an ocean pollution visualization inspired by Minesweeper.

sections.content: The studio brief was to create a visualization that responded to real-time data. I chose ocean plastic waste and looked for an interaction that could make its scale tangible.

Players try to uncover the blue tiles while avoiding the red ones. The twist is that the number of red tiles is set by the amount of plastic waste in the oceans. With the data updating live, the increasing difficulty becomes part of the message.
Rubaan Singh created the tile illustrations. Plastic Sweeper was featured in the p5.js 2020 showcase as one of three selected projects from India.
